R0069.title: Upload Abuse
R0069.definition: Using a business system's normal file upload functionality to upload unexpected files.
R0069.description: Business systems with user-generated content features such as image or file uploads can be exploited by attackers who upload files through the upload interface that are not intended for the platform's normal use, but rather for illegal storage, distribution of illegal content, and other purposes.
R0069.influence: Consumes platform storage and network resources, and may create compliance risks.

observables: A single account issues high-frequency, large-file upload requests through the upload interface, with storage usage growth far exceeding normal business levels
Uploaded file types do not match the business purpose (e.g., a real-name verification endpoint receives non-ID images or video slices)
Returned upload URLs are heavily hotlinked by external sites, generating large amounts of bandwidth consumption from non-platform sources
Content uploaded by a single account is aggregated via URLs into a playable sliced video resource

R0069-001.title: Image Hosting Abuse
R0069-001.definition: Users upload images or files through the platform's normal image upload feature that are not intended for the site's normal functions, and abuse the resources for external access.
R0069-001.description: Two common scenarios: first, users upload large volumes of images to use the platform's image upload feature as personal cloud storage; second, users upload video files disguised as images. Users slice video files into segments, append each segment to an image file to disguise them as images, upload the sliced files via the image upload interface, and use an m3u file to aggregate the image URLs for video playback. This is common in features that allow immediate image upload and return a URL, such as ID photo upload before identity verification or avatar upload after account creation. If the page is not finally submitted, it typically bypasses backend review, creating a blind spot that can be exploited to distribute pirated or pornographic videos.
R0069-001.influence: Disrupts normal system operations, consumes large amounts of network bandwidth and storage space, and creates compliance risks.

references.title: Remote Image Hosting Service Gradually Shutting Down

observables: The avatar or ID-photo upload endpoint receives large volumes of image uploads from a single account that never completes the final submission step
Uploaded image files have anomalous data appended to their ends, and the URLs can be combined via an m3u file to play back video
External access to uploaded images is heavy and concentrated on external video sites or cloud-drive contexts
A single account's storage usage is severely inconsistent with normal business profiles (e.g., thousands of images stored via an ID-photo endpoint)

R0069-002.title: Cloud Storage Abuse
R0069-002.definition: Similar to image hosting abuse (R0069-001), but the difference is that cloud storage is a feature of the business's cloud service rather than an ancillary resource for user-generated content.
R0069-002.description: Using the cloud storage feature provided by the business to upload unexpected or illegal content. Cloud storage may be part of a cloud computing service or a cloud drive, and is typically subject to weaker content moderation than user-generated content, making it potentially exploitable by bad actors to distribute pirated or pornographic videos.
R0069-002.influence: Disrupts normal system operations, consumes large amounts of network bandwidth and storage space, and creates compliance risks.

references.title: Alibaba OSS Storage Bucket Breached, Malicious Shell Scripts Distributed via Steganography

observables: A cloud storage bucket or object store shows abnormally high write volume from a single account, with file types mostly videos or compressed archives
External link requests for distributing pirated or pornographic videos, where content moderation is weak, concentrate on specific storage paths
Cloud-drive features are used to store non-business files, with external sharing volumes far exceeding normal user behavior
Storage costs diverge significantly from the actual user-growth curve
